turns.prompt: In standard (GIL-enabled) CPython, two threads each run counter += 1 100,000 times on a shared global counter, with no lock. Why can the final value be less than 200,000? In CPython the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) ensures that only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so the two threads cannot interleave their increments and no updates are lost. Because the GIL serialises the execution, you would get exactly 200 000 without needing any additional synchronization. If you rewrote the same logic with asyncio, the two coroutines would also run on the same thread and, since there is no `await` inside the increment, they would never be pre‑empted, giving the same correct result.

follow_ups.answer: `counter += 1` is a read‑modify‑write sequence, and the GIL only protects individual bytecode instructions, not the whole operation. While one thread holds the GIL, another thread can be scheduled between the bytecode that loads the current value and the bytecode that stores the incremented value, so two threads may read the same value and one increment gets overwritten, causing the final count to be less than 200 000. Using a `threading.Lock` (or an atomic type) around the increment makes the whole read‑modify‑write atomic and guarantees the correct total. In asyncio all coroutines run on a single thread and the event loop switches contexts only at `await` points; because the increment contains no `await`, it cannot be pre‑empted, so no race occurs there. Races can still appear in async code if a read and a write are separated by an `await`, but not in this pure‑CPU increment.
